newsitem.title: UK: Britain promises urgent law review over West film.
newsitem.headline: Britain promises urgent law review over West film.

text.p: The British government promised an urgent review the law on Thursday after one of its legal officials prompted protests by selling the rights to a movie about the life of serial killers Fred and Rosemary West.
A government minister in the office of the Lord Chancellor -- the country's top judge -- said limits could be placed on the "commercial exploitation or glorification" of mass murderers.
Protests erupted after it emerged that the Official Solicitor, the legal official in charge of the West estate, had decided to sell the rights to West's memoirs to a film company.
"(The Lord Chancellor and I) both felt this cannot be right. It does not feel right, and therefore we need to urgently review this law," minister Gary Streeter told BBC radio.
One newspaper said the company at the heart of the storm had dropped plans to make the film but Streeter made clear the review would go ahead, although he stressed Harris had done nothing wrong.

"What we need to look at is whether there should be some limit to the commercial exploitation or glorification of the sort of monstrous deeds that have happened in the Fred West case," he told BBC radio.

The duties of the Official Solicitor -- a post currently held by Peter Harris -- include looking after the interests of children, the mentally ill and others who are unable to represent themselves in court proceedings.

West's older brother Doug said the deal was "sick" and Caroline Roberts, who was sexually abused by the Wests when she was their nanny, said she was worried about what it would do to victims' families.
Fred West was found hanged two years ago in a prison cell where he was awaiting multiple charges of murder.

Many of his victims' bodies were found buried in the garden and cellar of his home at 25 Cromwell Street in Gloucester, western England -- a building so notorious that officials not only knocked it down but ground its bricks into dust.
Rosemary is now serving 10 life sentences for murdering girls and young women.

Harris on Tuesday confirmed that the London-based Portman group had acquired an option to make the film, saying it was his duty to "maximise the financial return to the estate" on behalf of West's five surviving children.
The option includes access to tape recordings of police interviews with West, tapes of his favourite blue movies and pages of his memoirs written when awaiting trial.
The Daily Express quoted John Banks, a director of the Portman Entertainment Group, as saying: "We will not be making the film." No one at Portman could be contacted for comment.
